newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Copyright experts tackle Internet piracy.
newsitem.headline: Copyright experts tackle Internet piracy.

text.p: Diplomats and industry leaders from more than 100 countries Monday began working on the first major revision of international copyright laws in 25 years with books, music and other intellectual property threatened by the advent of the Internet and cyberspace piracy.
"This is an attempt to settle problems caused by new technologies," said Alfons Schafers, Germany's representative to the three-week conference.

Copyright laws based on national boundaries have been made irrelevant by the fast, borderless world of the Internet, which acts as a giant copying machine where anything from music to software can be duplicated and distributed at the click of a computer mouse.

The gathering, the first in a quarter century, was organised by the World Intellectual Property Organisation, a United Nations agency which coordinates international patents, trademarks and copyrights.

Delegates to the conference are expected to approve three new treaties -- one for literary and artistic works, one for the rights of performers and a third for producers of databases -- to ensure the electronic transmission of any copyright work is subject to the same rules as paper and other physical copies.

The pacts will come under scrutiny from multibillion-dollar industries ranging from music production to computer databases, battling to keep profits against the high-tech information age revolution and for whom intellectual property is big business.

Adrian Strain of the London-based International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, which groups 1,100 record producers in more than 70 countries, said electronic delivery of music recordings could take a $2 billion share in the $40 billion-a-year global music business in coming years.
"Electronic delivery of music is itself a huge potential market for the recording industry," he said in an interview.
Some, however, have voiced concerns that some of the proposed safeguards go too far and could restrict the free flow of information and slow the growth of the Internet itself.
Once any new treaties are approved, the next question will be how to enforce them. In the multimedia world of Internet and its "copyright".

Once new treaties are passed, distribution of copyright work will be illegal. But new mechanisms will be needed to catch those who illicitly upload -- or distribute -- copyright material to the Net, say officials who hope national governments will pass laws to address the issue.
"There are gaps in the umbrella. But once these treaties are improved, it will clarify the situaation," said Mihaly Ficsor, assistant director general of the World Intellectual Property Organisation.
